example_incidents.summary: One of the largest U.S. commercial insurers was hit by a new variant of Phoenix CryptoLocker (attributed to the Russia-linked Evil Corp syndicate). Attackers accessed systems from March 5-21, 2021, exfiltrating data before deploying ransomware and knocking core systems offline, including remote access, email, and phone systems.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Reportedly paid $40 million in ransom - among the largest ransom payments publicly reported at the time. Full cost of remediation/legal/breach-notification beyond the ransom itself is not publicly disclosed in aggregate.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Attackers initially demanded $60 million; CNA paid approximately $40 million roughly two weeks after data theft began.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Multi-week disruption to remote access, corporate email, and phone systems; CNA stated it was able to recover encrypted/stolen data with no indication the exfiltrated data was viewed, retained, or shared further after payment.
example_incidents.data_impact: Corporate and some employee/customer data was copied/exfiltrated prior to encryption; CNA said no indication the data was subsequently misused, though the scope of records affected was not fully broken out publicly.

example_incidents.victim: Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) - U.S. broker-dealer/financial services unit
example_incidents.summary: LockBit compromised ICBC's U.S. financial-services division (believed via Citrix NetScaler vulnerabilities CVE-2023-4966/4967), disrupting settlement of U.S. Treasury trades and repo financing at the world's largest bank by assets - a rare ransomware incident with visible, market-wide operational impact.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not a disclosed single dollar loss figure for ICBC itself, but market-wide impact was measurable: more than $62 billion of U.S. Treasurys reportedly failed to deliver on one day, and settlement of over $9 billion in Treasury-backed assets was disrupted.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: No ransom amount publicly confirmed as demanded or paid by ICBC.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: ICBC's unit lost access to corporate email and had to physically courier settlement details via USB stick to counterparties in Manhattan while systems were restored; disruption lasted several days before normal electronic settlement resumed.
example_incidents.data_impact: Data exfiltration/theft was claimed by LockBit but the specific volume/type of records taken was not comprehensively disclosed publicly.

example_incidents.summary: A Fortune 500 title-insurance and real-estate services provider (handles closings for a large share of U.S. home sales) had systems taken offline for about a week; ALPHV/BlackCat claimed the intrusion, and the gang's removal of FNF from its leak site is widely interpreted as a sign a ransom was paid.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Specific dollar cost of the incident (remediation, business interruption, legal) not publicly broken out by FNF; real estate closings nationwide were delayed for the outage period, an indirect economic impact not quantified publicly.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: No official ransom figure disclosed by FNF; ALPHV's swift removal of FNF from its leak site is widely read by researchers as an indicator a payment was made, but this is inference, not confirmed disclosure.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Systems were offline for nearly a week, disrupting title/escrow closings for home buyers and real estate agents nationwide during that period.
example_incidents.data_impact: Data of approximately 1.3 million individuals was confirmed stolen and subject to breach notification.

example_incidents.country: United Kingdom (global client base incl. U.S., Europe)
example_incidents.summary: A UK-based financial software vendor whose platforms underpin derivatives clearing/trading for major banks and brokers was hit by LockBit, forcing at least 42 clients - including major U.S. and European financial institutions - to fall back to manual trade processing for cleared derivatives.
example_incidents.financial_impact: No public disclosure of direct financial loss to ION or its clients; the incident's significance was systemic/operational (derivatives clearing workflow disruption) rather than a disclosed dollar figure.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: LockBit threatened to publish stolen data by February 4, 2023 if unpaid; no ransom amount or payment/non-payment was publicly confirmed by ION.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Affected servers were isolated and the incident contained to a specific environment; several days of manual/workaround trade processing for affected clients while remediation continued.
example_incidents.data_impact: LockBit claimed data was exfiltrated during the intrusion; scope/type of data was not comprehensively disclosed publicly by ION.

example_incidents.summary: A U.S. banking-as-a-service (BaaS) bank whose infrastructure underpins numerous fintech apps (e.g., Affirm, Wise, Mercury) was breached after an employee clicked a malicious link; Evolve refused to pay, so LockBit published the stolen data, exposing both direct banking customers and downstream fintech partner customers - a clear third-party/supply-chain risk case for the sector.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Specific dollar cost not publicly disclosed by Evolve; the company offered two years of free credit monitoring/identity protection to affected individuals, an ongoing cost not quantified publicly. Reputational/partner-relationship impact on its fintech clients was significant but not dollar-quantified.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Evolve confirmed it did NOT pay the ransom demand (amount not publicly disclosed), leading LockBit to publish the stolen data.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Attackers accessed and downloaded data from Evolve's databases/file shares over a window from February to May 2024 before the bank discovered the intrusion in May 2024; public notification did not begin until July 8, 2024.
example_incidents.data_impact: At least 7.6 million individuals' personal data affected, including names, Social Security numbers, bank account details, card PANs, wire/settlement files, in clear text; downstream fintech partners (Affirm, Mercury, Wise, and others) were also impacted.

example_incidents.date: Disclosed June 9, 2026; Qilin claimed responsibility June 22, 2026
example_incidents.summary: Libya's central bank disclosed a cyberattack affecting a limited number of systems/technical services; the Qilin ransomware-as-a-service operation later publicly claimed the breach and threatened to release confidential banking data, illustrating ransomware's expansion into national financial-infrastructure/central-bank targets.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed. The bank characterized the incident as affecting only a limited set of systems, with no reported disruption to national payment operations.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: No ransom amount publicly disclosed or confirmed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Bank stated the incident was 'fully contained' as of late June 2026, with recovery/system restoration ongoing per an internal plan; no extended public-facing outage reported.
example_incidents.data_impact: Qilin threatened to release confidential banking data but as of the incident's public reporting, the specific volume/type of data was not independently confirmed or publicly itemized.

example_incidents.victim: Frost Bank and Citizens Financial Group (Citizens Bank) - shared third-party vendor breach
example_incidents.summary: The Everest ransomware gang claimed breaches of two unrelated major U.S. banks, Frost Bank (San Antonio) and Citizens Financial Group, tracing back to a single shared third-party vendor that handled statement printing (for Citizens) and tax-document fulfillment (for Frost) - a textbook example of concentrated third-party/vendor risk in the financial sector, since one vendor compromise exposed customers of multiple unrelated institutions.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed by either bank in dollar terms; both institutions face customer class-action lawsuits alleging inadequate safeguarding of data via the vendor relationship, with litigation costs not yet quantified publicly.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: No ransom amount publicly disclosed; Everest gave a six-day deadline before threatening to publish the full data dump.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Both banks stated their own core systems were not directly breached (the incident occurred in the third-party vendor's environment); no extended outage of banking services was reported.
example_incidents.data_impact: Everest claimed roughly 250,000 Frost Bank client records (Social Security numbers, tax IDs, names, mortgage rates, investment/income data, home addresses) and additional Citizens Bank records, with combined exposure reported by researchers at up to approximately 3.65 million records across both institutions.

example_incidents.victim: Deutsche Bank (via third-party marketing/incentive platform vendor)
example_incidents.summary: The 'Unsafe' ransomware-as-a-service group added Deutsche Bank to its leak site, posting screenshots purporting to show database exports (employee emails, password hashes, mailing addresses). Deutsche Bank clarified the actual incident occurred at an external German service provider operating a marketing/incentive platform for the bank's sales partners, not within Deutsche Bank's own core banking environment - another illustration of third-party/vendor exposure at a major global bank.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: No disruption to core Deutsche Bank banking services reported; investigation of the third-party provider's environment was ongoing at time of disclosure.
example_incidents.data_impact: Group claimed employee email addresses, password hashes, and physical mailing addresses among the exposed records; scope limited to data held within the third-party marketing/incentive platform rather than core customer banking data, per Deutsche Bank's statement.

Managed IT/security service providers and outsourced call centers

Regulatory reporting and financial-market-utility interfaces

subcategories: Online and mobile banking/insurance portals

Email and collaboration systems
Call center and customer service platforms

hazard_categories.description: How ransomware actors most commonly gain their initial foothold into financial and insurance institutions and their third-party ecosystems.
subcategories: Exploitation of internet-facing remote-access appliances (e.g., Citrix NetScaler CVE-2023-4966/4967 in the ICBC incident)
Phishing and malicious links leading to credential/endpoint compromise (e.g., Evolve Bank & Trust employee click)
Stolen/leaked credentials sourced from infostealer logs (54% of ransomware victims per 2025 Verizon DBIR had prior credential exposure)
Compromise via a shared/downstream vendor rather than the institution's own perimeter (Frost/Citizens shared vendor; Deutsche Bank marketing-platform vendor)
Exploitation of unpatched known CVEs in edge/VPN infrastructure
Business email compromise as a precursor to ransomware deployment

hazard_categories.description: The specific pressure mechanisms ransomware groups apply against financial and insurance victims, who are unusually sensitive to both downtime and disclosure.
subcategories: Encryption of core systems to force operational downtime (classic single extortion)
Data exfiltration and double extortion (threat of publishing stolen customer/financial records - dominant pattern in nearly all example incidents above)
Leak-site countdown deadlines to pressure fast payment (e.g., Everest's 6-day deadline on Frost/Citizens)
Harassment of executives, customers, or regulators directly (naming institutions publicly, contacting affected customers)
Reputational/'shaming' posts calling out incident-response vendors or refusal to negotiate (ALPHV's public post against FNF)
Threats of onward sale of data to third parties rather than public leak, as a middle-ground pressure tactic (MAPFRE/Lapsus$)

hazard_categories.description: A hazard category distinct to this industry: ransomware against a single financial institution or vendor can cascade into broader market or payment-system disruption well beyond the immediate victim.
subcategories: Disruption to trade clearing/settlement causing failed deliveries at a market level (ICBC: $62B+ in failed Treasury settlements in a single day)
Derivatives/clearing platform outages forcing manual processing across many institutions simultaneously (ION Group affecting 42+ clients)
Central bank/national payment infrastructure targeting with potential monetary-policy or public-confidence implications (Central Bank of Libya)
Contagion through banking-as-a-service and fintech partner networks, where one bank's compromise exposes many unaffiliated fintech brands' customers (Evolve Bank & Trust)

hazard_categories.description: Given heavy outsourcing of processing, document fulfillment, and technology in this sector, a large share of recent notable incidents originate outside the named institution's own network.
subcategories: Concentrated vendor risk - a single vendor compromise affecting multiple unrelated financial institutions (Frost Bank + Citizens Bank via shared print/fulfillment vendor)
Core processor/payments vendor compromise (Fiserv, TSYS-type entities appearing as ransomware group targets)
Fintech/BaaS partner-network exposure cascading to end consumers who never had a direct relationship with the breached entity
Marketing/loyalty platform vendors handling employee or partner data on the institution's behalf
Weak contractual/audit visibility into subcontractors' security posture (a recurring theme in post-incident litigation, e.g., GLBA vendor-accountability suits against Citizens/Frost)

hazard_categories.description: Ransomware incidents in finance and insurance trigger a dense, sector-specific web of regulatory obligations that amplify cost and compress response timelines relative to other industries.
subcategories: Breach notification regimes with short/compressed timelines (contributing to elevated 'detection & escalation' cost share per IBM 2025 - ~34% in financial services vs ~29% global)
Sector-specific regulatory regimes (GLBA in the U.S., DORA in the EU, functional-regulator rules for banks/insurers)
SEC disclosure obligations for material cybersecurity incidents (as invoked in the FNF SEC filing)
State/national data-protection authority investigations (e.g., Spanish AEPD scrutiny in MAPFRE's 2021 incident)
Follow-on class-action litigation from affected customers, increasingly targeting both the breached entity and its vendors

hazard_categories.description: How ransomware-driven downtime specifically manifests in financial and insurance operations, which are unusually time-sensitive and trust-dependent.
subcategories: Loss of access to trading/settlement systems forcing manual, error-prone workarounds
Branch, call-center, and digital-channel outages affecting customer-facing service availability
Delayed real estate closings/title transactions when escrow/title systems are down (FNF)

subcategories: Single-employee phishing susceptibility as a root cause (Evolve Bank & Trust)

overview: Finance and insurance is one of the most consistently targeted industries in the ransomware threat landscape, combining three features attackers prize: high-value, tightly regulated data (PII, account/payment details, claims and underwriting data); low tolerance for downtime given real-time payment, trading, and claims obligations; and deep interdependency through vendors, fintech partners, and market infrastructure that lets a single compromise cascade well beyond one victim. Recent ransomware.live data (100 most-recent sector-tagged victims, spanning roughly April-July 2026) shows the sector being hit across the full spectrum of institution types - community banks and credit unions, insurers and brokers, wealth/asset managers, fintech and payments firms, and even a central bank - by a wide range of groups (Qilin, Everest, DragonForce, Akira, Everest, LockBit successors, Lapsus$, and newer entrants like Unsafe and Krybit), with double-extortion (encrypt-and-exfiltrate) now the dominant pattern. Notable historical and recent incidents illustrate two especially distinctive hazards for this industry versus others: (1) systemic/market-contagion risk, where ransomware against a market-infrastructure or processing vendor (ICBC, ION Group) disrupts trading and settlement across many unaffiliated institutions simultaneously, and (2) concentrated third-party/vendor risk, where a single shared vendor breach (Frost Bank/Citizens Bank's shared document-fulfillment vendor, Deutsche Bank's marketing-platform vendor, Evolve Bank & Trust's BaaS/fintech-partner network) exposes customers of multiple otherwise-unrelated financial brands at once. Authoritative industry reporting (Sophos, IBM, Coveware, Verizon DBIR) consistently ranks financial services among the highest-cost, highest-ransom-demand sectors, while regulatory regimes (GLBA, DORA, SEC disclosure rules) compress response timelines and add materially to breach cost relative to most other industries.

Healthcare and Social Assistance is one of the most heavily targeted sectors in the ransomware ecosystem, driven by a combination of low tolerance for downtime (patient safety), high-value PHI, fragmented and legacy IT/OT environments, and a long tail of small, under-resourced providers (clinics, home health agencies, billing firms) alongside a handful of giant, deeply interconnected health systems and claims processors. Ransomware.live's "Healthcare" sector tag currently lists 2,443 posted victims spanning 2015-2026 (dataset pulled 2026-07-19/20), with the pace of incidents accelerating sharply since 2020 (34 in 2020 vs. 627 in 2025 and 387 already in the first ~6.5 months of 2026). The threat-actor landscape is fragmented across 206 distinct named groups in the dataset, with Qilin (178), LockBit3 (143), Inc Ransom (128), BianLian (92), RansomHub (81), Clop (72), ALPHV/BlackCat (68), Everest (63) and Medusa (63) the most prolific against this sector. Geographically the US dominates (1,092 recorded victims), followed by the UK (58), Australia (58), Canada (57), India (56), Germany (55), France (47) and Brazil (45), reflecting both the concentration of large private health systems in the US and the global reach of double-extortion groups. Industry-wide cost data consistently shows healthcare as the single costliest sector for data breaches (IBM: ~$7.4M average per breach in 2025, down from ~$9.8M in 2024 but still #1 of all industries for the 14th consecutive year), even as 2025 ransom demands and payments in healthcare specifically have fallen sharply (Sophos/Coveware both report demands down roughly 90% from 2024's average and healthcare among the least likely sectors to pay). The single largest loss event on record for the sector by far is the February 2024 Change Healthcare/UnitedHealth Group attack, whose total company-reported impact reached roughly $2.9 billion for fiscal year 2024 alone, disrupting an estimated one-third of all US patient medical records and claims processing nationwide via a critical, deeply embedded third-party clearinghouse — illustrating the sector's acute concentration/third-party-dependency risk.

hazard_categories.description: How ransomware operators first gain a foothold in healthcare and social-assistance environments, which tend to run large numbers of internet-facing legacy systems, remote-access tools for clinicians/vendors, and understaffed security teams.
subcategories: Exploitation of unpatched, internet-facing VPN/remote-access appliances and edge devices (a leading Verizon DBIR-cited vector for healthcare breaches, up sharply year over year)

Compromised or purchased VPN/RDP/Citrix credentials, including credentials harvested by infostealer malware from employee or third-party devices (ransomware.live 'infostealer' telemetry shows large stealer-log exposure tied to healthcare victims, e.g. Medibank)
Phishing and business-email-compromise targeting clinical, billing, and admin staff
Compromise of managed service providers (MSPs), IT vendors, and EHR/practice-management software resellers who hold privileged access across many small provider networks
Exploitation of vulnerabilities in widely-deployed healthcare-adjacent software (file-transfer tools, VoIP/telehealth platforms, backup software) as mass 'one-to-many' entry points
Insider-enabled access or credential sale by disgruntled or compromised employees/contractors

hazard_categories.description: The specific pressure mechanisms ransomware groups use against healthcare targets, which are unusually effective against this sector because of patient-safety stakes and the sensitivity of medical data.
subcategories: Encryption of clinical, administrative, and financial systems (EHR, PACS, pharmacy, lab, scheduling) forcing 'downtime procedures' and patient diversion

Data exfiltration and double/triple extortion — publishing or threatening to publish stolen PHI on leak sites (roughly three-quarters of recent healthcare cases reportedly involve exfiltration, per Coveware)

Targeted harassment of especially vulnerable patients using stolen sensitive records (e.g., ALPHV/BlackCat's publication of nude cancer-patient treatment photos at Lehigh Valley Health Network; Medibank attackers publishing abortion and addiction-treatment records) to increase payment pressure
Direct extortion emails/calls to patients or plan members threatening individual data release unless the organization (or the individual) pays
DDoS attacks layered on top of encryption/exfiltration to pressure incident-response teams
'Re-victimization' — re-posting or re-selling the same stolen healthcare dataset by multiple groups or brokers after an initial attack (dispossessor/second-hand leak listings observed in the dataset)

hazard_categories.description: Healthcare is unusually dependent on a small number of concentrated technology and services intermediaries (claims clearinghouses, pathology/lab partners, billing processors, EHR vendors), making single points of failure catastrophic and systemic.
subcategories: Claims clearinghouse / revenue-cycle processor compromise (Change Healthcare/Optum — processes ~15 billion transactions/year, roughly a third of US patient records, per reporting) causing nationwide billing and pharmacy disruption far beyond the direct victim
Pathology, lab, and diagnostic-services partner compromise (Synnovis attack on NHS London trusts) halting blood testing and surgeries at hospitals that never touched the attacker directly
EHR, practice-management, and medical-billing software vendor compromise cascading to hundreds of downstream clinics/practices
Managed IT/security services provider compromise granting simultaneous access to many hospital or clinic networks
Business-associate and vendor risk under HIPAA — breach liability extending to the covered entity even when the incident originates at a subcontractor
Group-purchasing, supply, and medical-device-maintenance vendors as pivot points into hospital networks

hazard_categories.description: Unlike most sectors, ransomware in healthcare directly threatens physical patient safety through disruption of connected medical equipment and clinical workflows, not just IT/data confidentiality.
subcategories: Forced downtime/diversion of ambulances and emergency departments during EHR outages (documented at UHS 2020 and other hospital-system attacks)
Disruption of networked medical devices, infusion pumps, imaging/PACS systems, and lab analyzers that depend on now-encrypted or isolated networks
Delayed or cancelled surgeries, chemotherapy, dialysis, and elective procedures during recovery windows
Documented contribution to patient harm/death from care delays (UK Coroner findings tied delayed blood-test results after the Synnovis attack to a patient death)
Reversion to paper-based/manual clinical documentation for weeks, increasing medication and diagnostic error risk
OT/IT convergence risk in hospital facilities systems (HVAC, building access, refrigeration for pharmaceuticals/blood products)

hazard_categories.description: Healthcare carries some of the heaviest breach-notification, privacy, and liability regimes of any industry, amplifying the downstream cost of a ransomware event well beyond technical remediation.
subcategories: HIPAA/HHS OCR breach notification, investigation, and potential civil monetary penalties (US)
State attorney-general actions and multistate settlements
Mass tort / class-action litigation from affected patients (e.g., $65M Lehigh Valley Health Network settlement; CommonSpirit and HCA class actions)
GDPR and equivalent international health-data protection regimes for multinational providers and insurers
Government/parliamentary inquiries and mandatory incident reporting for public health systems (Ireland's HSE, UK NHS)
Loss of accreditation, payer contract, or Medicare/Medicaid compliance risk tied to prolonged system unavailability
Cyber-insurance coverage disputes and sub-limits given the scale of potential claims in this sector

hazard_categories.description: The sector's large, high-turnover clinical and administrative workforce, broad system-access footprint, and understaffed security teams create distinct human-layer exposure.
subcategories: Widespread, broad EHR access privileges among clinical staff increasing blast radius of a single compromised account
Credential reuse and shadow-IT tools (e.g., unsanctioned messaging/file-sharing apps used by clinicians) bypassing security controls
Chronic cybersecurity staffing/budget shortfalls relative to IT complexity, especially at rural hospitals, nursing homes, and behavioral-health/social-assistance providers
Third-party staffing and locum/travel clinician access management gaps
Social engineering of help-desk/password-reset workflows (a rising vector per 2025-2026 reporting, including at Change Healthcare-adjacent and other large-health-system incidents)

example_incidents.group: ALPHV/BlackCat (initial encryption/exfiltration); RansomHub (subsequent extortion/data listing after an alleged 'exit scam' by ALPHV affiliates)
example_incidents.date: Attack began February 21, 2024; disclosed February 2024; extortion/data-listing activity continued into April 2024
example_incidents.summary: The largest and most disruptive healthcare ransomware incident on record. Attackers used compromised credentials to access a Citrix portal lacking multi-factor authentication, then deployed ransomware against Change Healthcare, the dominant US claims clearinghouse processing roughly one-third of all patient records and ~15 billion transactions annually. The outage froze prescription processing, insurance eligibility checks, and provider payments nationwide for weeks.
example_incidents.financial_impact: UnitedHealth Group's total reported cyberattack impact reached approximately $2.9 billion for fiscal year 2024 (direct response costs plus business disruption); an initial Q1 2024 estimate of $0.74/share grew through the year to a full-year estimate of $1.90-$2.05/share. UnitedHealth also advanced more than $9 billion in interim/interest-free funding to affected providers by Q2 2024 to offset cash-flow disruption across the industry.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: UnitedHealth confirmed paying a ransom reported by multiple outlets at roughly $22 million in bitcoin to the ALPHV/BlackCat affiliate; a second group (RansomHub) subsequently claimed to still hold the stolen data and re-extorted the company.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Core clearinghouse and pharmacy/claims systems were down for multiple weeks beginning February 21, 2024, with a phased, multi-month restoration of full transaction volumes through spring 2024.
example_incidents.data_impact: UnitedHealth later disclosed the breach affected the personal/health information of approximately 190 million individuals (one of the largest healthcare data breaches ever reported to HHS), including medical records, billing/claims data, SSNs, and insurance information.

example_incidents.victim: Universal Health Services (UHS) — ~400 US hospitals/care sites
example_incidents.summary: One of the earliest large-scale hospital-system ransomware attacks; Ryuk encrypted IT systems across UHS's national network, forcing staff onto paper documentation, diverting ambulances, and suspending IT applications company-wide.
example_incidents.financial_impact: UHS reported approximately $67 million in total pre-tax losses tied to the attack (lost operating income, reduced patient activity, billing-delay reserves, and recovery costs), and stated it expected to recover most of this through cyber insurance.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: UHS did not pay a ransom and recovered from backups; no confirmed ransom amount was publicly reported.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: EHR and other core IT applications were down across all ~400 UHS care sites for roughly three weeks before full restoration.
example_incidents.data_impact: No large-scale confirmed public data leak was widely reported for this incident (Ryuk at the time was primarily an encryption-only/non-exfiltration operation); primary impact was operational/clinical disruption rather than a mass PHI leak.

example_incidents.victim: Health Service Executive (HSE) — Ireland's national public health system
example_incidents.summary: A nationwide ransomware attack that forced Ireland's entire public health IT infrastructure offline, disrupting hospital appointments, cancer treatment scheduling, radiology, and COVID-19 vaccine registration systems across the country. Conti later provided a free decryptor under international pressure but retained and later leveraged stolen patient data.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Estimates for recovery costs varied widely across reporting: the HSE's director general cited a June 2021 estimate exceeding $600 million; other analyses put full recovery cost at roughly $100 million, and yet other reporting cited about $83 million; figures differ by scope (pure IT rebuild vs. total health-system impact) and are not fully reconciled in public reporting.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Conti demanded $19,999,000; the HSE refused to pay and instead worked with Ireland's National Cyber Security Centre; a free decryptor was later released by the attackers.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: National IT systems were shut down immediately upon detection; full recovery across the health system took approximately four months.
example_incidents.data_impact: Patient data was exfiltrated and reportedly used to attempt individual extortion of patients; Ireland's HSE has since (as of reporting around 2025) offered approximately EUR750 in compensation to affected individuals whose personal data was compromised.

example_incidents.victim: CommonSpirit Health — ~140+ hospitals across ~13 US states
example_incidents.group: Unattributed publicly at the time (not clearly listed under a named leak-site group in available tracking)
example_incidents.date: Initial access September 16, 2022; ransomware detected/disclosed October 2-3, 2022
example_incidents.summary: One of the largest US nonprofit hospital operators was forced to take systems offline across more than 100 facilities in at least 13 states, delaying access to EHRs and disrupting patient care, following network compromise weeks before the ransomware deployment was detected.
example_incidents.financial_impact: CommonSpirit initially estimated the cost at approximately $150 million, later revising the total to approximately $160 million (business interruption, remediation, and related expenses) as reported in 2023 disclosures.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Multi-week system outages beginning October 2022 affecting more than 100-160+ facilities; precise full-recovery date not specified in public reporting.
example_incidents.data_impact: Personal data of more than 623,700 patients was reported exposed; the breach affected over 150 facilities and led to two class-action lawsuits.

example_incidents.summary: Attackers compromised a network supporting a Lackawanna County physician practice, including a radiation-oncology imaging system, and — after LVHN refused to pay — published highly sensitive clinical photos of breast cancer patients (nude from the waist up) to pressure payment, an unusually aggressive harassment-based extortion tactic.
example_incidents.financial_impact: LVHN agreed to a $65 million class-action settlement (finalized November 2024), one of the largest healthcare ransomware-related settlements on record; of this, $52 million was earmarked for patients whose nude treatment images were published.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: LVHN refused to pay the ransom; the specific dollar amount demanded was not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Specific system-downtime duration not publicly detailed in available reporting; the affected system was a specific practice's oncology imaging network rather than network-wide LVHN infrastructure.
example_incidents.data_impact: More than 134,000 patients were affected/eligible for settlement compensation; leaked data included sensitive treatment photographs and other PHI published on BlackCat's leak site.

example_incidents.group: REvil-affiliated actor (Aleksandr Ermakov, later sanctioned by Australia)
example_incidents.date: Attack detected October 2022; extortion/data leaks began November 2022
example_incidents.summary: Attackers stole and threatened to publish highly sensitive personal and health data of Medibank's customers, including records revealing abortions, addiction treatment, and mental-health conditions, after the insurer refused a ransom demand — one of Australia's largest ever data breaches and a landmark case in international ransomware attribution/sanctions.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not fully quantified in a single public figure in the sources reviewed; the incident drove significant remediation, regulatory, and reputational costs and a multi-year AFP-led international investigation; precise total company cost not publicly disclosed in the sources found.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Initial demand of roughly US$10 million (A$15 million), later reduced to approximately US$9.7 million; Medibank refused to pay, consistent with Australian government guidance against ransom payments.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Primarily a data-theft/extortion event rather than an encryption/operational-outage event; core insurance operations were not reported as extensively down.
example_incidents.data_impact: Personal and health data of approximately 9.7 million current and former customers was compromised, including about 1.8 million international customers; data included Medicare, passport, and driver's licence numbers plus sensitive medical history.

example_incidents.victim: Synnovis (pathology/blood-testing partner for NHS trusts in London)
example_incidents.summary: A ransomware attack on a third-party pathology provider partnered with Guy's and St Thomas' and King's College Hospital NHS Trusts caused a critical shortage of O-negative blood, cancelled thousands of appointments and procedures, and was later formally identified as a contributing factor in a patient death — one of the clearest documented cases of ransomware causing loss of life via a healthcare supply-chain/third-party vector.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Specific total financial cost to Synnovis or the NHS trusts was not found publicly quantified in a single disclosed figure in the sources reviewed; disruption was extensive across South-East London NHS services for months.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Severe disruption began June 3, 2024, with over 11,000 outpatient/elective procedure appointments delayed; some services were affected for months, with normal service levels reported restored by December 2024 — roughly six months.
example_incidents.data_impact: Qilin published approximately 400GB of stolen data on June 20, 2024, including patient names, NHS numbers, and descriptions of blood tests.

overview: The Information Technology sector (software vendors, IT-services/MSPs, SaaS/cloud hosts, distributors, semiconductor/EDA and telecom-adjacent firms) is one of the two most-targeted industries in ransomware, consistently ranking behind only manufacturing. Its defining risk feature is systemic/aggregation exposure: IT companies sit upstream of thousands of downstream customers, so a single intrusion into an MSP platform (Kaseya), a managed file-transfer product (MOVEit/Progress), a SaaS provider (CDK Global), or a distributor (Ingram Micro) cascades into mass downstream outages and data loss far larger than the direct victim. Beyond encryption-based extortion, the sector is disproportionately exposed to data-theft/leak extortion and intellectual-property theft (source code, chip designs, product blueprints). Common initial-access paths are the sector's own internet-facing edge (VPNs, RMM tools, MFT appliances), leaked/infostealer credentials, and exploitation of vulnerabilities in products the companies themselves ship. Regulatory exposure is intensifying (SEC cyber-disclosure rules, GDPR, breach-notification statutes, and large class-action liability). Sector-level economics per Sophos 2025 and IBM 2025: technology accounts for roughly 9% of ransomware incidents; the average technology-sector data-breach cost is about $4.79M, and the average ransomware/extortion incident costs about $5.08M.

subcategories: Exploitation of internet-facing/VPN and edge appliances (e.g., Palo Alto GlobalProtect at Ingram Micro, Fortinet/Citrix, Microsoft Exchange as used against Acer)
Exploitation of managed file transfer / edge software (MOVEit, GoAnywhere, Accellion) for mass exfiltration
Leaked or purchased credentials and infostealer logs (initial-access-broker marketplaces)
Abuse of remote monitoring & management (RMM) and remote-access tooling
Phishing / social engineering of admins and developers
Exploitation of zero-day/n-day vulnerabilities in the vendor's own shipped products, turning the product into an attack vector against customers

hazard_categories.description: IT firms face the full multi-extortion playbook; data-theft and source-code/IP leak threats are especially potent because reputation and confidentiality are core to the business.
subcategories: Encryption of production, build/CI-CD and virtualization (VMware ESXi) systems
Data exfiltration and public leak-site publication (double extortion)
Triple/quadruple extortion: DDoS and direct harassment of the victim's downstream customers, partners and employees
Threatened disclosure of source code, product blueprints and signing keys/certificates
Ransom escalation and event-timed pressure (e.g., REvil publicizing Quanta/Apple leak during Apple's launch event)

hazard_categories.description: The signature hazard of the IT industry: because these firms are technology suppliers, a single compromise propagates to their entire customer base, creating catastrophic aggregation/accumulation risk for insurers.
subcategories: MSP/RMM platform compromise cascading to managed clients (Kaseya VSA -> up to ~1,500 downstream businesses)
SaaS/hosted-platform outage cascading to customer operations (CDK Global -> ~15,000 dealerships)
Distribution/reseller channel disruption halting downstream commerce (Ingram Micro order processing)
Software-supply-chain / trojanized-update or embedded-product-vulnerability propagation (MOVEit -> 2,700+ organizations)
Cloud/subprocessor concentration and single-points-of-failure shared across many tenants

subcategories: Product designs and hardware blueprints (Quanta/Apple device schematics)
Semiconductor / chip design and EDA data (ARM, Synopsys as recent leak-site claims)
Proprietary source code and algorithms
Code-signing keys, certificates and secrets enabling further supply-chain abuse
Trade secrets, roadmaps and confidential customer contracts

hazard_categories.description: Dependence on shared infrastructure and a dense web of subprocessors amplifies both the likelihood and blast radius of incidents.
subcategories: Shared cloud/hosting infrastructure and multi-tenant architecture
Subprocessor and nested-vendor dependency chains
Data-processor liability for downstream clients' data held on behalf of customers
Concentration of many customers on one platform (systemic insurer accumulation risk)

hazard_categories.description: IT breaches trigger outsized legal and disclosure consequences given the volume of third-party data and public-company status of many victims.
subcategories: SEC cyber-incident disclosure obligations and investigations (SEC probe of Progress Software/MOVEit)
GDPR and global breach-notification statutes across many jurisdictions
Mass class-action litigation (MOVEit spawned dozens of suits, 40M+ claimants)
Contractual SLA penalties, indemnities and customer breach-of-contract claims
Cross-border data-transfer and sovereignty complications

example_incidents.summary: REvil exploited zero-day vulnerabilities in Kaseya's VSA remote-monitoring-and-management software to push ransomware through ~60 direct MSP customers to their downstream clients — the archetypal IT supply-chain cascade attack.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Direct financial loss to Kaseya not publicly disclosed; downstream impact spanned 800-1,500 businesses across ~17 countries (e.g., Sweden's Coop grocery chain closed ~800 stores). Broader economic cost not authoritatively quantified.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: REvil demanded a single universal-decryptor payment of $70 million in Bitcoin. Kaseya states it did NOT pay the ransom; it obtained a universal decryptor from a 'trusted third party' (later reported as provided via the FBI).
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: VSA SaaS and on-prem servers taken offline as a precaution on July 2; patched VSA restored around July 11-12; a universal decryptor was distributed on July 22-23, 2021 to help victims restore data. Recovery for downstream MSP clients ran days to weeks.
example_incidents.data_impact: Primarily encryption/availability impact rather than mass data theft; up to ~1,500 downstream organizations had systems encrypted.

example_incidents.summary: Clop mass-exploited a zero-day SQL-injection flaw (CVE-2023-34362) in Progress Software's MOVEit managed-file-transfer product to steal data from thousands of organizations worldwide — one of the largest supply-chain data-extortion campaigns on record.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Aggregate downstream cost estimated by Emsisoft at roughly $10.6B-$15.8B (using IBM's per-record cost); some scaled estimates ran far higher. Progress Software's own direct costs not fully disclosed; it faced an SEC investigation and dozens of class-action lawsuits (40M+ claimants).
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Clop did not encrypt systems; it demanded extortion payments from individual victim organizations (amounts varied and were not publicly itemized). Many victims declined to pay.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: This was a data-theft (not encryption) event, so impact was breach-remediation and notification rather than operational downtime; remediation and victim-notification stretched over many months into 2024.
example_incidents.data_impact: Over 2,700 organizations confirmed impacted and approximately 93.3 million individuals' personal data exposed (estimates ranged 64M-95M+ over time).

example_incidents.summary: BlackSuit ransomware crippled CDK Global's Dealer Management System SaaS, which powers operations for ~15,000 auto dealerships across the U.S. and Canada; a second intrusion during recovery on June 19 prolonged the outage.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Anderson Economic Group estimated total dealer losses exceeding $1 billion (revised up from ~$944M) from roughly two-plus weeks of disruption.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: BlackSuit initially demanded ~$10M, reportedly escalating toward $50M+. CDK is widely reported to have paid approximately $25 million in Bitcoin (wallets tied to BlackSuit received ~$25M about two days after the attack, per CyberScoop).
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Dealerships reverted to manual/pen-and-paper processes for nearly two weeks; CDK announced services restored for nearly all dealerships by around July 4, 2024.
example_incidents.data_impact: Primarily operational outage; extent of any data exfiltration less publicly quantified than the operational and financial disruption.

example_incidents.summary: SafePay ransomware caused a global outage at Ingram Micro, one of the world's largest IT distributors; intrusion is attributed to compromised credentials on the Palo Alto GlobalProtect VPN, halting worldwide order processing.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Specific revenue loss not publicly disclosed; multi-day global halt of order processing at a distributor with ~$48B annual revenue implies material lost/delayed transactions, though the company did not quantify it publicly.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Ransom amount not publicly disclosed; on July 29-30, 2025 SafePay threatened to leak ~3.5TB of allegedly stolen data unless paid. No confirmation of payment.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Systems failed around 8:00 AM ET on July 3; website and staged order processing resumed July 7-8; the company reported operations back to normal worldwide by July 9, 2025.
example_incidents.data_impact: Reported exposure of personal data of over 42,000 employees and applicants; SafePay claimed ~3.5TB of data.

example_incidents.summary: After Quanta (a major Apple ODM) declined to pay, REvil pivoted to extort Apple directly, publishing stolen schematics for unreleased products, timed to Apple's 'Spring Loaded' launch event — a landmark IP-theft extortion in the tech hardware supply chain.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed. Impact was primarily reputational and IP-confidentiality loss (leaked device blueprints) rather than reported revenue loss.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: REvil demanded $50 million, reportedly escalating toward $100M; the ransom was not paid by Quanta (and REvil eventually removed the leaked files). No confirmed payment.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Operational downtime not the primary reported impact; this was chiefly a data-exfiltration/IP-leak extortion event.
example_incidents.data_impact: Theft and partial publication of confidential design schematics/blueprints for unreleased Apple devices (MacBook, Apple Watch drawings).

example_incidents.summary: Clop ransomware struck German enterprise-software giant Software AG, encrypting internal systems and stealing about 1TB of data, then publishing files after the company refused to negotiate — an early high-profile double-extortion case in the software industry.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Direct financial loss not fully disclosed; the company reported internal-network disruption but said customer-facing cloud services were unaffected.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Clop demanded approximately $23 million. Software AG refused to pay.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Internal network, help desk and some internal communications were disrupted for a period in October 2020; customer cloud services remained operational.
example_incidents.data_impact: About 1TB of data stolen, including employee passport/ID data, health-related documents and internal emails; screenshots and files leaked publicly after negotiations broke down.

example_incidents.summary: Hunters International claimed a January 2025 ransomware attack on Tata Technologies (engineering/IT-services arm of the Tata group), later leaking 1.4TB of stolen data; Tata Motors disclosed a ransomware incident to Indian stock exchanges.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed; the company said client-delivery services remained unaffected. No quantified revenue loss reported.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Specific ransom amount not disclosed; Hunters International threatened public release of the data and, when unpaid, leaked it (~730,000 files) on its dark-web site in March 2025.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Temporary disruption to some IT services per the January stock-exchange disclosure; client delivery reported unaffected. Detailed recovery timeline not publicly quantified.
example_incidents.data_impact: Claimed theft of 1.4TB (~730,000 files) including current/former employee personal details, purchase orders and confidential customer contracts (India and U.S. customers).

example_incidents.summary: One of the most consequential OT-impacting ransomware attacks in manufacturing history; the global aluminum producer was forced into manual/paper-based operations across dozens of plants after LockerGoga encrypted IT systems that also touched production processes. Norsk Hydro refused to pay the ransom and publicly disclosed the incident in near-real time, becoming a widely cited case study in transparent incident response.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Total financial impact reached approximately $70-75 million, per Norsk Hydro's own quarterly financial disclosures; initial Q1 2019 losses were estimated at $35-41 million with additional Q2 losses of $23-29 million.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Ransom amount not publicly disclosed by attackers in a fixed figure; Norsk Hydro refused to pay the ransom entirely and rebuilt systems from backups instead.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Several aluminum extrusion plants were forced to switch to manual operations for an extended period; full IT recovery took multiple weeks, with the company reporting it was still not at 100% normal operations several weeks after the attack. Microsoft's incident response team was brought in to assist recovery.
example_incidents.data_impact: Primarily an availability/encryption event rather than a large-scale data-exfiltration/extortion case (LockerGoga predates widespread double-extortion); no large trove of stolen customer data was reported leaked.

example_incidents.summary: EKANS ransomware, one of the first ransomware strains purpose-built to target ICS/OT process-control software, hit Honda's internal network, forcing production and sales halts at multiple plants worldwide (Japan, US, UK, Turkey, Brazil, India, and elsewhere). Likely initial access was via an exposed RDP connection.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as a specific dollar figure by Honda; industry analyses characterize the loss as significant given multi-day, multi-plant global production stoppage but no official cost figure was released.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed; no confirmed ransom payment reported.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Production and sales of cars, motorcycles, and power/marine products was suspended at plants across multiple countries for several days before systems were restored; exact recovery timeline varied by site.
example_incidents.data_impact: Primarily an OT/production-availability event; no large confirmed customer data leak was publicly reported in connection with this specific 2020 incident.

example_incidents.summary: Electronics-manufacturing giant Foxconn's Mexico facility was hit over the Thanksgiving 2020 weekend; attackers encrypted roughly 1,200 servers, exfiltrated data, and destroyed a large volume of backups before demanding a very large ransom.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as an official incident-cost figure by Foxconn; the destruction of 20-30 TB of backup data materially increased recovery cost and complexity beyond the ransom figure itself.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: DoppelPaymer demanded 1,804.0955 BTC, reported at the time as approximately $34 million (some sources cite ~$32.97 million); Foxconn did not pay, and stolen data was later published on the dark web.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Foxconn confirmed the ransomware disrupted production operations at the affected Mexico facility; precise recovery timeline in days not independently confirmed in public reporting beyond confirmation that normal operations were eventually restored.
example_incidents.data_impact: Approximately 100 GB of unencrypted files were stolen prior to encryption (double-extortion); 20-30 TB of backup data was deliberately deleted by the attackers to hamper recovery.

example_incidents.summary: The Snatch ransomware/extortion group claimed to have breached a Volvo Cars file repository and stole a portion of the automaker's proprietary R&D data, leaking sample files as proof. Volvo disputed being a 'victim of ransomware' per se, framing it as unauthorized third-party access to one file server, but confirmed R&D data theft.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed; Volvo did not report a specific financial cost figure for the incident.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed; no confirmed ransom demand amount or payment reported. Volvo stated it maintained control of its data and did not indicate paying any ransom.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: No significant production/operational downtime was publicly reported; this was primarily a data-theft/extortion event rather than an OT-disruptive encryption event.
example_incidents.data_impact: Snatch leaked approximately 35.6 MB of sample stolen R&D files as proof of the larger theft; Volvo stated it saw no indication of impact to customer safety, vehicle security, or personal customer data.

example_incidents.country: United States (Latin America/North America plants affected)
example_incidents.summary: The tire and rubber manufacturer detected a security incident in late February 2022; LockBit 2.0 claimed responsibility on March 11, 2022, and threatened to publicly release stolen business and customer data unless a ransom was paid. Bridgestone proactively disconnected manufacturing and retreading facilities across North and Latin America to contain the incident.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as an official total-cost figure; Bridgestone engaged Accenture Security for incident response, adding external forensic/recovery costs on top of ~10 days of idled production across ~30 plants.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Specific ransom demand amount not publicly disclosed; Bridgestone did not confirm payment, and LockBit proceeded to leak stolen data after the deadline passed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Approximately 30 plants across North America and Latin America were shut down for about 10 days; all plants had resumed normal operations by March 9, 2022.
example_incidents.data_impact: Business records were accessed and stolen, including files containing Social Security numbers, bank information, and other sensitive data belonging to some customers.

example_incidents.summary: The German automotive-parts giant was breached via an employee's browser download; LockBit gained access to internal systems and, after negotiations broke down, publicly offered the stolen dataset for sale on its leak site for a headline figure of $50 million (later reduced to $40 million).
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as an official incident-cost figure by Continental beyond confirming systems access occurred; no confirmed operational-loss figure released.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: LockBit publicly listed the stolen data for sale at $50 million on November 9, 2022, reduced to $40 million by November 29, 2022; negotiation transcripts published by LockBit show discussions beginning September 23, 2022, but Continental has stated it aborted contact with the group rather than paying.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: No major manufacturing/plant downtime was publicly reported; this was chiefly a data-exfiltration/extortion event rather than an OT-encryption event.
example_incidents.data_impact: Attackers claimed to have stolen roughly 40 terabytes of internal files (some early reports mis-stated this as 40 GB), including technical documents and source code, based on screenshots published on the leak site.

example_incidents.summary: A single server managed by Yamaha's Philippines motorcycle-manufacturing/sales subsidiary was breached and hit with ransomware; INC Ransom added the company to its leak site roughly three weeks later and published stolen employee and corporate data.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Yamaha stood up a countermeasures team and launched an investigation; no specific downtime duration was publicly disclosed, and the impact was described as limited to one server.
example_incidents.data_impact: Approximately 37 GB of allegedly stolen data was published, including employee ID information, backup files, and corporate/sales information; partial leakage of employees' personal information was confirmed by Yamaha.

example_incidents.summary: Nissan detected an intrusion into its Australian division's network in December 2023; the Akira ransomware gang claimed responsibility and, after negotiations reportedly failed, threatened to leak stolen business and personal data. Nissan confirmed in 2024 that the breach affected roughly 100,000 individuals across Australia and New Zealand, including customers, dealers, and current/former employees.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as an official cost figure by Nissan.

overview: Manufacturing has been the single most-targeted sector by ransomware operators for five consecutive years through 2025, driven by a combination of high operational-downtime sensitivity (which pressures victims toward paying quickly), widespread reliance on legacy OT/ICS equipment with long refresh cycles, deep tiered supply-chain interdependency that multiplies contingent business-interruption exposure, and valuable intellectual property/trade-secret data. The ransomware.live "Manufacturing" sector tag alone contains 4,434 recorded victim postings, with year-over-year posting volume roughly quadrupling from 2021 (295) to 2025 (1,204), and the sector accounting for an estimated one in four ransomware attacks globally by 2025 per industry trackers. Attack economics are shifting: per Sophos's 2025 manufacturing-specific report, successful encryption rates have fallen sharply (74% to 40% YoY) as defenses improve, but attackers are compensating by shifting toward pure data theft and extortion, and average ransom demands against manufacturers have risen even as median demands/payments across all sectors trend down. High-profile incidents — from Norsk Hydro's ~$70M LockerGoga attack (2019) through Honda's global OT-targeted Snake/EKANS shutdown (2020), Foxconn Mexico's $34M DoppelPaymer demand (2020), Bridgestone's 30-plant, 10-day shutdown (2022), Continental's 40TB data-theft/$50M extortion (2022), and Nissan Australia's 100,000-person PII breach (2023) — illustrate the sector's dual exposure to both OT-driven physical-production disruption and conventional IT-driven data-theft/extortion, often within the same threat-actor toolkit.

industry: Professional, Scientific, Technical Services, Real Estate and Wholesale Trade
overview: This composite industry group spans consultancies, IT/managed services, law and accounting firms, engineering firms, staffing and BPO providers, travel management companies, commercial real estate services, and wholesale/logistics distributors. Ransomware.live's 'Business Services' sector tag is one of the most heavily populated on the platform, logging dozens of new claimed victims per week in mid-2026, with RaaS/extortion groups Qilin, DragonForce, INC Ransom, TheGentlemen, Akira, RansomHouse, Deadlock, and data-extortion crews like ShinyHunters posting new victims almost daily. The sector's risk profile is distinctive because these firms sit at a structural chokepoint: (1) they hold sensitive, often privileged or regulated client/third-party data (legal, financial, M&A, PII) that amplifies extortion leverage; (2) many are themselves suppliers/vendors (MSPs, SAP integrators, BPOs, staffing firms, travel managers) whose compromise cascades into downstream client organizations, making them attractive 'one-to-many' targets; and (3) wholesale trade/logistics operations depend on time-sensitive order, warehouse, and freight systems where even short outages create cascading supply-chain and revenue impact. Reported financial impact ranges enormously by incident type - from multi-hundred-million-dollar remediation and litigation costs at large diversified BPOs (Conduent) and IT consultancies (Cognizant, Sopra Steria) down to smaller professional firms where impact is mostly data-exposure/breach-notification driven rather than large ransom payments. Across the sector, exfiltration-only and SaaS/CRM (e.g., Salesforce) compromise via vishing/social engineering has become as common a threat vector as classic file-encryption ransomware.

overview: Public administration — national ministries, state/provincial agencies, and city/county/municipal governments, plus public libraries, courts, and administrative boards — is one of the most heavily and persistently targeted sectors for ransomware. Governments are attractive targets because they run large, heterogeneous, and often under-funded legacy IT estates; hold vast quantities of citizen PII and sensitive records; deliver essential, hard-to-suspend public services (911/emergency dispatch, tax and revenue collection, benefits, permitting, courts, utilities billing); and are politically visible, which raises the pressure to restore service quickly. Unlike private firms, governments frequently refuse to pay ransoms as a matter of policy — so the dominant financial exposure is not the ransom itself but the downstream cost of downtime, forensic investigation, system rebuild/replacement, credit monitoring for affected citizens, and legal/notification obligations, which routinely run many multiples of the original demand (e.g. Atlanta ~$17M vs a ~$51K demand; Baltimore ~$18M vs a ~$76K demand; Columbus $7.3M recovery vs a $1.9M demand refused). The sector also faces a distinctive blend of financially-motivated ransomware-as-a-service crews (Royal, Rhysida, Play, LockBit, BlackCat/ALPHV, Interlock, Medusa) and, at the national level, state-nexus actors where extortion and espionage overlap. Double- and triple-extortion (encryption plus data leak plus public shaming/notification of citizens) is now standard, making even well-backed-up governments vulnerable to reputational and privacy harm. From a cyber-insurance standpoint, the sector is characterized by high attack frequency, high aggregate downtime/recovery loss, moderate-to-low ransom-payment rates, strong dependence on third-party MSPs and shared statewide systems (systemic/aggregation risk), and significant regulatory and public-accountability exposure.

example_incidents.summary: Conti hit nearly 30 Costa Rican government institutions including the Ministry of Finance (Hacienda), CCSS social security fund, MICITT, labor ministry, and state ISP RACSA. On 8 May 2022 President Rodrigo Chaves declared a national state of emergency and characterized it as an act of terrorism/'war' - the first time a country declared a national emergency over ransomware. Tax collection, customs, and public services were paralyzed.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Economic drag estimated at ~$38 million per day of downtime; the Costa Rican Chamber of Foreign Commerce estimated losses exceeding $125 million in the first two days alone (halted tax/customs). Costa Rica invested ~$25 million in recovery; the U.S. State Department pledged $25 million in March 2023 to aid recovery and cyber-capacity building.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Conti demanded US$10 million, later doubled to US$20 million; the government declined to pay.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Critical systems (Hacienda, CCSS) disrupted for weeks to months; a second wave (attributed to HIVE) hit the CCSS health system on 31 May 2022, forcing manual operations across hospitals. Recovery spanned months with international assistance.
example_incidents.data_impact: Data exfiltrated from the Ministry of Finance and other bodies; Conti published stolen data on its leak site when the ransom was refused.

example_incidents.summary: SamSam ransomware crippled City of Atlanta systems, taking down online bill-pay, court systems, and numerous municipal applications. A landmark early municipal ransomware case; two Iranian nationals (Faramarz Shahi Savandi and Mohammad Mehdi Shah Mansouri) were indicted by the U.S. DOJ in November 2018.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Recovery ultimately cost approximately $17 million (a confidential report figure), roughly six times the initial ~$3M estimate. Break-down: ~$6M initial response, ~$11M to repair/replace damaged systems, desktops, laptops and devices. The city had initially budgeted ~$6M.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Attackers demanded about $51,000 (roughly 6 bitcoin) in total; Atlanta did not pay.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Multiple departments were down or degraded for days to weeks; some systems and data were never fully recovered, and years of police dashcam footage were lost.
example_incidents.data_impact: Numerous applications and records affected; some data permanently lost (e.g. police dashcam video). Broad operational data loss rather than a quantified PII count.

example_incidents.summary: On 7 May 2019 RobbinHood ransomware took most of Baltimore's government systems offline (all servers except essential services). Email was down, forcing employees to use personal Gmail; property transfers and the water-billing/payment systems were frozen, disrupting the real-estate market.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Estimated ~$18 million total: ~$10 million to restore/rebuild systems plus ~$8 million in lost or deferred revenue.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Attackers demanded 13 bitcoin (~$76,000-$80,000 at the time); Mayor Bernard 'Jack' Young refused to pay.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Recovery, initially expected to take weeks, ultimately extended from May into roughly September 2019 (~4 months) for full restoration.
example_incidents.data_impact: Widespread system encryption; disruption to city databases and payment/records systems. No large single PII-breach count is the headline - impact was primarily operational.

example_incidents.summary: The Royal ransomware gang attacked the City of Dallas in May 2023, disrupting critical services including 911 dispatch systems, police/court operations, and city websites. One of the most significant U.S. municipal attacks of 2023.
example_incidents.financial_impact: The city approved roughly $8.5 million in costs to remediate and recover from the attack (downtime/response costs).
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: No ransom payment was publicly reported/confirmed as paid; ransom demand not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Multiple systems, including 911/CAD and municipal court operations, were disrupted for weeks; restoration efforts continued over several weeks into the summer of 2023.
example_incidents.data_impact: More than 27,000 current and former employees and their dependents were notified that their personally identifiable information was exposed in the attack.

example_incidents.summary: Rhysida struck the City of Columbus in July 2024. The city refused to pay and, notably, sued a security researcher who publicized the leaked data - drawing national attention to how governments handle post-breach disclosure.
example_incidents.financial_impact: The city spent about $7.3 million on recovery, including ~$2.4M for forensics/remediation/data-mining, ~$1.6M for Experian identity-theft protection, and ~$1.95M for legal counsel.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Rhysida demanded about $1.9 million (~30 bitcoin); Columbus refused to pay, after which the group leaked stolen data.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: City services and systems were disrupted for weeks; recovery and remediation extended over months, with continued identity-protection provisioning for affected residents.
example_incidents.data_impact: Large volume of resident and employee data exposed and partially leaked (including data tied to crime victims and city employees); the city offered Experian identity-theft protection to affected individuals (hundreds of thousands).

example_incidents.summary: On 28 October 2023 Rhysida attacked the British Library (a UK public/national institution), taking down its website, catalogue, and public Wi-Fi. Described as 'one of the worst cyber incidents in British history'; the Library refused to pay and the attackers leaked the stolen data.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Recovery expected to consume roughly 40% of the Library's financial reserves - about £6-7 million (~$7.5-9M) - far exceeding the ransom demanded. Follow-on rebuild tenders (e.g. ~£400,000) continued into 2024-2025.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Rhysida demanded 20 bitcoin (~£596,000 / ~$750,000 at the time); the Library did not pay.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Severe disruption for months; the main catalogue returned in read-only form on 15 January 2024, with many services degraded well into 2024. Full rebuild extended over more than a year.
example_incidents.data_impact: Approximately 600GB / nearly 500,000 files exfiltrated - much from the CRM database - including personal data of Library users and staff; ~600GB was publicly dumped when the ransom was refused. ~20,000 authors/illustrators had Public Lending Right payments delayed.

example_incidents.summary: A cyberattack beginning 25 July 2025 hit the City of St. Paul so severely that the Minnesota National Guard was activated to assist. The mayor confirmed it as a ransomware attack by the Interlock ransomware-as-a-service group. Core systems - internal networks, online payment portals, and public Wi-Fi - were disrupted.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as a total figure as of reporting; response involved state resources and the National Guard, indicating substantial cost.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: The city stated it would not pay the ransom; specific demand amount not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Core city systems were down and progressively restored over weeks following the July 25 onset; the National Guard's involvement reflected the complexity of recovery.
example_incidents.data_impact: After the city refused to pay, Interlock publicly posted approximately 43GB of data stolen from St. Paul.

example_incidents.summary: Federal and state authorities investigated a ransomware attack that disrupted key services across the State of Nevada in August 2025, interrupting multiple government services including phone systems and state agency websites - illustrating the escalation of ransomware to the U.S. state-government level.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed at time of reporting.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Multiple state services - phone systems and agency websites - were interrupted; recovery handled with federal (CISA/FBI) assistance over the following days/weeks.
example_incidents.data_impact: Under investigation at time of reporting; data-theft impact not fully quantified publicly.
