example_incidents.group: DragonForce (attack attributed to the "Scattered Spider" affiliate cluster)
example_incidents.summary: One of the most disruptive retail ransomware incidents on record. Attackers used social-engineering (help-desk/Active Directory compromise) to encrypt core systems; DragonForce contacted M&S's CEO directly via a hacked employee email account. M&S was forced to shut down automated ordering, stock and click-and-collect systems for weeks, reverting to pen-and-paper processes for fresh food and clothing supply.
example_incidents.financial_impact: M&S disclosed total incident costs of £101.6 million (£82.7m incident response/recovery, £18.9m third-party costs); the company guided to roughly £300 million of lost operating profit for FY2025/26; statutory pre-tax profit fell from £391.9m to £3.4m over the affected half-year; the attack wiped an estimated £750 million off M&S's market capitalization at its worst point.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly confirmed whether M&S paid; DragonForce publicly claimed the encryption/extortion but no verified payment amount has been disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Online ordering and click-and-collect were suspended for roughly 6-7 weeks; full operational recovery of automated stock/ordering systems took months.
example_incidents.data_impact: Customer personal data (names, contact details, order history, dates of birth) was confirmed stolen; M&S stated payment card details were not compromised.

example_incidents.date: April 2025 (disclosed publicly in stages through mid-2025)
example_incidents.summary: Part of the same UK retail campaign that hit M&S and Harrods. DragonForce exfiltrated data via third-party/network access, then escalated to a direct extortion threat via Microsoft Teams and a phone call to Co-op's head of security. Co-op proactively disconnected systems to head off a ransomware deployment, which limited operational disruption relative to M&S but did not stop the data theft.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Co-op reported £206 million in lost revenue attributable to the incident in its official earnings disclosure.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: DragonForce demanded payment for the stolen member data; Co-op has not disclosed paying a ransom, and the UK National Crime Agency arrested four suspects (aged 17-20) in July 2025 on Computer Misuse Act, blackmail, and money-laundering charges.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Systems were proactively taken offline to contain the threat; the company described a multi-week restoration process for affected back-office and membership systems.
example_incidents.data_impact: Personal data of all 6.5 million Co-op members was confirmed stolen (names, dates of birth, emails, phone numbers, home addresses); no financial/payment card data was taken.

example_incidents.victim: CDK Global (SaaS/DMS provider to ~15,000 US/Canada auto dealerships - third-party supply-chain incident affecting the retail auto sector broadly)
example_incidents.summary: BlackSuit ransomware hit CDK Global, the dominant dealer management system (DMS) provider for North American car dealerships, forcing an industry-wide outage. A second attack during initial recovery on June 19 further delayed restoration. Nearly 15,000 dealerships had to revert to manual, paper-based sales, financing, and service workflows for close to two weeks - a textbook example of concentrated third-party/supply-chain risk in the retail sector.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Anderson Economic Group estimated total financial damage to dealers at just over $600 million in the first two weeks of the shutdown alone - roughly 24 times the ransom paid.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Attackers initially demanded $10 million, escalating to $50 million; blockchain analysis (TRM Labs) traced approximately 387 BTC (~$25 million) to a BlackSuit-linked wallet on June 21, 2024, consistent with a paid ransom, though CDK never officially confirmed payment.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Dealer systems were down for nearly two weeks; CDK restored services in a phased rollout through late June/early July 2024.
example_incidents.data_impact: Not publicly detailed at the individual-record level; primary reported impact was operational (sales, financing, service scheduling) rather than a disclosed mass PII leak.

example_incidents.summary: Scattered Spider used a 10-minute vishing call to MGM's IT help desk (via LinkedIn-sourced employee impersonation) to obtain Okta admin credentials, then handed off to ALPHV/BlackCat for ransomware deployment. MGM chose not to pay and rebuilt systems from backups, causing days of casino, hotel, and slot-machine outages across its Las Vegas properties.
example_incidents.financial_impact: MGM disclosed a $100 million negative impact on Q3 2023 results, comprising approximately $84 million in lost revenue (from disrupted hotel, casino and online operations) and $10 million in one-time technology consulting, legal, and third-party advisory expenses.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: MGM stated it never considered paying and did not pay a ransom.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Core systems (reservations, digital key cards, slot machines, ATMs) were down for roughly 10 days; full operational recovery took several weeks.
example_incidents.data_impact: Customer personal information (names, contact details, dates of birth, driver's license and Social Security/passport numbers for some customers) was confirmed stolen.

example_incidents.summary: Scattered Spider socially engineered a third-party IT support vendor for Caesars' identity provider (Okta) to gain network access, exfiltrating loyalty-program customer data before deploying an extortion threat. Unlike MGM, Caesars opted to negotiate and pay, prioritizing avoiding a public data leak and minimizing operational disruption.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not broken out publicly as a discrete total-cost figure (unlike MGM); reported impact centered on the ransom payment and associated incident-response/legal costs, which were not separately quantified in public filings.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Attackers initially demanded $30 million; Caesars paid approximately $15 million in cryptocurrency to prevent publication of stolen data.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Caesars avoided the extended, highly visible operational outages MGM experienced, largely because it paid quickly and did not have hotel/casino systems encrypted in the same way.
example_incidents.data_impact: Loyalty program (Caesars Rewards) database exposed, including driver's license numbers and, for a significant number of members, Social Security numbers.

example_incidents.date: Compromise reported mid-2025; extortion/leak threats through June 2026
example_incidents.summary: Part of a broad ShinyHunters campaign that used voice-phishing (vishing) against corporate help desks to trick employees into authorizing a malicious connected app in Salesforce, then exfiltrated data via a modified Salesforce Data Loader - a pure data-extortion attack with no encryption payload, illustrating the sector's growing SaaS/CRM exposure.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed by Ralph Lauren as a discrete cost figure.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: ShinyHunters issued a public leak deadline as extortion leverage; no confirmed ransom payment amount has been reported.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: No significant operational/store downtime reported - this was a data-theft/extortion event rather than an encryption/availability incident.
example_incidents.data_impact: More than 220 GB of data claimed stolen, including customer information, transaction records, and documents related to unreleased future product lines.

example_incidents.victim: Madison Square Garden Sports Corp. (parent of the New York Knicks; consumer/entertainment services)
example_incidents.summary: Same ShinyHunters Salesforce-vishing campaign as Ralph Lauren/JCPenney. Attackers socially engineered access to MSG's client/talent CRM database using the old-fashioned vishing technique, then claimed a very large-scale data theft spanning customers, staff, and celebrities/former players.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Extortion/leak-deadline threat issued by ShinyHunters; no confirmed payment reported.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: No reported operational outage - data-theft/extortion event, not an encryption event.
example_incidents.data_impact: ShinyHunters claimed roughly 26 million records, including 9.8 million emails, ~9,500 dates of birth, and close to 5 million street addresses/full names/phone numbers; a leaked "Talent" file reportedly included former Knicks players/coaches, MSG executives' family members, and celebrities.

example_incidents.date: Unauthorized access before March 27, 2026; discovered April 4, 2026
example_incidents.summary: A regional single-location car dealership example (contrasted with the CDK/M&S/MGM enterprise-scale cases) illustrating that ransomware targets consumer-services retailers across the full size spectrum, not just national chains. RansomHouse claimed encryption of dealership systems.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not disclosed by RansomHouse or the dealership; Karl Auto Group stated it "did not pay ransom money."
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Phone and computer systems were unavailable over the Easter weekend (roughly April 4-8, 2026 and reportedly beyond, per public customer-facing social media posts); an outside forensic firm was engaged and the FBI/FTC were notified.
example_incidents.data_impact: Data exposed reportedly included full names, Social Security numbers, driver's license/government ID numbers, financial account information, and passport numbers/images; the number of affected individuals was not disclosed.

example_incidents.victim: PChome (pchome.com.tw) / NetHome Group and subsidiary Bibian
example_incidents.date: Claimed June 10, 2026; disclosed publicly late June 2026
example_incidents.summary: A major Taiwanese e-commerce/payment platform targeted by the emerging Settra group, illustrating ransomware risk to online-retail and embedded-payment infrastructure outside the US/UK. The parent company publicly disputed that its core systems were breached, while an affiliated subsidiary (Bibian) confirmed a related, separate data breach - a useful example of attacker claims vs. victim denial/dispute dynamics common in this sector.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: PChome stated its main platforms and payment channels continued operating normally with no evidence of an actual breach to core systems; no confirmed outage was reported.
example_incidents.data_impact: Settra claimed approximately 102GB of internal data stolen, including personal information for roughly 3.5 million members, nine years of operational records, system architecture diagrams, and employee personnel files; subsidiary Bibian separately confirmed exposure of member names, phone numbers, addresses, and purchase history, which reportedly led to follow-on phishing campaigns against customers.

overview: Retail Trade and Consumer Services (ransomware.live's "Consumer Services" sector tag) is one of the highest-volume ransomware targeting categories, spanning everything from single-location dealerships, gyms, and jewelry shops up to multinational department-store chains, casino/hospitality operators, and the shared SaaS platforms (CRM, dealer-management systems) that underpin the industry. A live pull of the ransomware.live sector feed (~120 victim postings across roughly a 2-month window in mid-2026) shows the sector is dominated by high-volume, opportunistic ransomware-as-a-service groups (Qilin, TheGentlemen, SafePay, DragonForce, Akira, Nova, Settra) hitting mostly small/mid-size retailers, HVAC/home-services firms, funeral homes, and franchise operations, alongside a smaller number of large, named-brand victims. Layered on top of this baseline is a distinct and increasingly dominant pattern: pure data-extortion campaigns against enterprise SaaS/CRM platforms (the ShinyHunters Salesforce-vishing campaign hit Ralph Lauren, JCPenney/Catalyst Brands, and Madison Square Garden Sports Corp. in 2025-2026) that steal customer and employee data without ever deploying encryption. The sector's most financially destructive incidents, however, remain operational-shutdown events: Marks & Spencer's 2025 DragonForce/Scattered Spider attack cost over £100m directly and roughly £300m in lost operating profit after weeks of manual, pen-and-paper store operations; the 2024 CDK Global (BlackSuit) attack on a shared auto-dealer platform caused an estimated $600m in dealer losses against a reported $25m ransom; and the 2023 MGM Resorts/Caesars Entertainment (Scattered Spider/ALPHV) attacks on hospitality/gaming caused a combined $100m+ loss and a confirmed $15m ransom payment, respectively. Sophos's 2025 retail-specific survey confirms the trend lines visible in these cases: 58% of retailers paying when hit, rising ransom demands (median $2M) alongside a falling encryption rate (48%, a five-year low) as attackers shift toward pure exfiltration, and the highest "lack of in-house security expertise" root-cause rate of any sector surveyed - consistent with a highly distributed, thin-security-staff, high-turnover industry that is unusually exposed to help-desk social engineering and third-party/franchise concentration risk.

data_source_notes:
Primary source (ransomware.live) worked but required discovery: the documented endpoint pattern /v2/victims/sector/{sector} 302-redirects to /apidocs/ and does not return data on the current v6.0-beta ('Aegis') API; the working endpoint is /v2/sectorvictims/Telecommunication (confirmed against /v2/sectors, which lists 'Telecommunication': 357). Also hit the stated 1-req/min rate limit once (got {"message":"1 per 1 minute"}) and succeeded on retry after waiting ~65s. Full 357-record JSON was pulled and parsed locally with jq for group/country/year aggregation.

Supplement 1 (ransomlook.io): partially worked. The documented `?query=` param returned "Query must be at least 2 characters" regardless of input; switching to `?q=` returned valid group-profile JSON with useful corroborating detail (used to confirm Arkana Security's WOW! attack and Babuk-Locker's telecom targeting).

Supplement 2 (ransomwhat.telemetry.ltd/posts.json): failed - the ransomwatch/ransomwhat project has been archived and the endpoint now serves a static "this project has been archived" HTML page rather than JSON, so no data was available from this source.

Where a reported figure could not be corroborated (e.g., WOW!/Cincinnati Bell/Colt precise financial cost), this is stated explicitly as "not publicly disclosed" rather than estimated.

example_incidents.summary: Argentina's largest telecom operator was hit by REvil ransomware that spread via a phishing email to a hijacked internal Domain Admin account, ultimately encrypting more than 18,000 workstations and disrupting internal systems including Office 365, OneDrive, corporate VPN, Citrix, Genesys and customer/field-service virtual machines.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: $7.5 million in Monero demanded, rising to $15 million after a 48-hour deadline passed. Telecom Argentina stated it contained the attack and regained access without paying.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Internal corporate systems (not customer-facing telecom/internet service) were disrupted; company said it isolated affected systems and restored operations using backups, without paying the ransom. Precise recovery timeline/cost not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed beyond the ransom demand itself; no confirmed customer-facing outage cost figures reported.
example_incidents.data_impact: Internal corporate/IT systems affected; no large-scale confirmed customer PII leak was publicly documented.

example_incidents.summary: US regional telecom/broadband provider Cincinnati Bell was listed as a victim on the Yanluowang ransomware group's leak site; the company publicly refused to pay the ransom.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Ransom amount not publicly disclosed; company confirmed it did not pay.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Specific downtime duration and recovery cost not publicly disclosed in available reporting.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed; no SEC filing or press disclosure of a specific dollar cost was located.
example_incidents.data_impact: Scope/type of data exfiltrated by Yanluowang not publicly detailed in available sources.

example_incidents.victim: Telecommunications Services of Trinidad and Tobago (TSTT)
example_incidents.summary: The Caribbean nation's state-owned telecom provider had an administrator's credentials compromised (October 3), leading to a security breach on October 9 that affected its internal virtual infrastructure/private cloud. RansomEXX later released a CSV of customer data on the dark web as proof of the hack.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Ransom amount not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: TSTT reported the breach affected availability of internal virtual infrastructure/private cloud; full recovery timeline not publicly quantified. CEO Lisa Agard was subsequently fired following the incident.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed. Trinidad and Tobago has no mandatory breach-notification law, which delayed and limited public cost disclosure.
example_incidents.data_impact: Over 1.2 million customer records (mobile, fixed line, broadband) leaked, including full names, emails, national ID numbers, phone numbers and ID scans; the leaked CSV was downloaded 13,000+ times within two weeks; TSTT internal GitLab projects and database dumps were also exposed.

example_incidents.summary: A newly-emerged data-extortion group, Arkana Security, breached major US cable/ISP WOW! after an employee's device was infected with infostealer malware in September 2024, harvesting credentials for backend platforms Symphonica and AppianCloud that gave attackers alleged full backend control (they released a demo video). This was Arkana's debut, high-profile attack.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: WOW! was given a deadline to negotiate or the data would be sold/leaked; specific dollar ransom demand not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: No confirmed customer-facing service outage reported; incident was primarily a backend data-access/exfiltration event rather than an encryption/downtime event.
example_incidents.financial_impact: In its March 28, 2025 SEC Form 8-K, WideOpenWest stated the incident had not had a material impact on operations and it did not believe it was reasonably likely to materially affect financial condition or results; the company also disputed that sensitive personal information was accessed, contrary to the attacker's claims.
example_incidents.data_impact: Arkana claimed theft of 403,000 WOW! user account records (names, usernames, salted passwords, emails, login histories, security Q&As) plus a separate CSV of 2.2 million records (names, addresses, phone numbers, device data).

example_incidents.group: Attributed on ransomware.live to 'coinbasecartel' data-extortion listing; technical intrusion used BPFDoor malware (attribution to a distinct ransomware crew is contested/unclear in public reporting)
example_incidents.summary: South Korea's largest mobile carrier (~23M subscribers) disclosed a breach of its Home Subscriber Server after detecting unusual traffic on April 22, 2025. Investigation found BPFDoor malware present undetected on at least 28 servers (33 variants) since as early as 2022, exfiltrating USIM authentication keys and other subscriber identifiers.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: No ransom payment publicly reported; this was primarily treated as a state-linked/criminal espionage-style data breach rather than a classic encryption ransomware case, though listed as a data-leak/extortion incident by dark-web trackers.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: No major network outage; SK Telecom offered free SIM replacements to all customers as remediation.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Record $97.2 million (KRW 134.8 billion) fine from South Korea's Personal Information Protection Committee, plus a ~$7,000 fine for late breach reporting; the Korea Consumer Agency separately ordered SK Telecom to pay ~$67 (100,000 won) compensation to each of the 23 million affected users; SK Telecom committed roughly $514 million to a security-overhaul 'Accountability and Commitment Program,' plus bill discounts, fee waivers and free data.
example_incidents.data_impact: 25 types of personal information for 23.2 million subscribers exposed, including phone numbers, IMSI numbers, and USIM authentication keys - raising SIM-swap and surveillance risk.

example_incidents.summary: Global business telecom provider Colt was breached via exploitation of the SharePoint remote-code-execution vulnerability CVE-2025-53770, leading to a multi-day (ultimately multi-week/multi-month) outage of Colt Online customer portal, hosting APIs, and Voice API/porting platforms; core network infrastructure reportedly remained largely unaffected. Colt publicly attributed responsibility to the WarLock ransomware group.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: WarLock demanded $200,000 for the stolen data cache and posted samples on dark-web forums as proof.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Outage began August 12, 2025; Colt stated the majority of recovery would take 8-10 weeks, with customer portal, hosting APIs and voice-on-demand tools still offline in early October 2025 - a multi-month recovery, unusually long for a major telecom provider.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Specific dollar cost of the incident not publicly disclosed by Colt; impact described qualitatively as affecting 27,000+ customers across ~40 countries.
example_incidents.data_impact: WarLock claimed theft of over one million documents including employee salary data, customer contact information, internal executive personal information, and confidential emails.

example_incidents.victim: Orange S.A. (Orange Group, incl. Orange Belgium subsidiary)
example_incidents.summary: French telecom giant Orange disclosed a security incident at the end of July 2025 involving internal systems, using the same SharePoint exploitation chain (webshells, Group Policy abuse, credential theft, lateral movement) attributed to WarLock. The group publicly claimed the attack on August 17, 2025 and released roughly 4GB of data. A separate, related incident hit Orange Belgium, affecting 850,000 customer accounts.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Specific ransom amount not publicly disclosed for the Orange S.A. incident.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Orange stated the attacker had only limited access and exfiltrated mostly 'outdated or low-sensitivity data'; no major prolonged network outage reported (unlike Colt).
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.data_impact: ~4GB of internal data published on the dark web by WarLock; Orange characterized the exposed data as largely outdated/low-sensitivity. The related Orange Belgium breach separately impacted 850,000 customer accounts.

example_incidents.summary: One of the world's largest cell-tower/telecom infrastructure REITs was breached in a 'pay-or-leak' extortion campaign by ShinyHunters. After American Tower did not pay by the group's June 15, 2026 deadline, the attackers published the stolen files - notable for exposing physical-security data (tower gate/access codes) rather than just customer records, illustrating the physical-infrastructure risk unique to telecom tower operators.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Extortion demand made; American Tower did not comply and data was leaked. Specific dollar figure not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: No network/tower service outage publicly reported; incident was a data-exfiltration/extortion event rather than an encryption/availability event.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as of this research.
example_incidents.data_impact: Attackers claimed over 5.2 million records including customer and landowner PII, records referencing other companies' infrastructure (T-Mobile, Verizon, US DHS), tower asset records with GPS coordinates, and plaintext physical access/gate codes for cell tower compounds; 216,601 accounts were added to Have I Been Pwned on June 26, 2026.

overview: The telecommunications sector - internet service providers, mobile network operators, fixed-line/cable carriers, tower/infrastructure companies, and satellite/media-adjacent telecom firms - has become an increasingly frequent ransomware and data-extortion target. Ransomware.live's own sector tracker lists 357 telecom-sector victims (tag "Telecommunication") with a pronounced acceleration in 2025-2026 (124 posted in 2025 alone, the sector's most active year on record, plus 62 more in the first ~7 months of 2026), corroborated by Cyble/Cybersecurity Dive research showing telecom ransomware attack volume grew roughly fourfold from 24 in 2022 to 90 in 2025. The threat-actor landscape is dominated by prolific double-extortion RaaS groups (Qilin, Akira, LockBit variants, Play, Clop) alongside a newer wave of pure data-extortion/leak-only crews with no encryption capability (Arkana Security, ShinyHunters, DragonForce) that specifically target telecom's dense stores of subscriber PII, SIM/USIM credentials, and call-detail metadata. What distinguishes telecom from most other industries in this taxonomy is the sector's dual exposure: (1) a large, regulated subscriber-PII attack surface comparable to healthcare or financial services, and (2) an "OT-equivalent" core-network/availability layer (HSS/HLR, BGP routing, voice/SMS switching, physical tower infrastructure) where a successful intrusion can cascade into regional or national service outages - as seen in incidents ranging from Vodafone Portugal's multi-day national outage to Cellcom's week-long US regional voice/SMS blackout. Third-party and supply-chain exposure is also unusually acute, given telecom's dependence on field-service subcontractors, MVNO/reseller relationships, shared backend SaaS platforms, and industry bodies - Verizon's 2025 DBIR found third-party involvement in 30% of all breaches, up sharply from roughly 15% the year before. Regulatory consequences have grown correspondingly severe, exemplified by SK Telecom's record $97.2M Korean privacy-regulator fine and mandated per-subscriber compensation after its 2025 USIM-data breach.

data_source_notes:
Base incident data (Step 1): The documented API v2 sector endpoint returned by ransomware.live's own docs (`/v2/victims/sector/{sector}` and variants like `/v2/sector/{sector}`) 404-redirected to the docs page. Cross-referencing the ransomware.live MCP server source code revealed the true route is `/v2/sectorvictims/{sector}`. However, this sector's tag literally contains a slash — "Transportation/Logistics" — and every encoding attempt tried (`%2F`, double-encoded `%252F`, `--path-as-is` curl flag, dash-substituted slug `Transportation-Logistics`, bare `Transportation`) either 404'd with the sector value truncated at the slash (server/router decodes %2F before route matching, so only "Transportation" reached the handler and no sector by that exact name exists) or hit the endpoint's "1 per 1 minute" rate limit (confirmed via a 429 `{"message":"1 per 1 minute"}` response on one attempt). Given the instructed retry-once-then-fallback policy, I fell back to WebFetching the equivalent live website page (https://www.ransomware.live/activity/Transportation-Logistics), which successfully returned real, current victim/group/date/country rows (500+ entries noted as available, ~20 most-recent shown) and served as the functional substitute for the raw API pull. The `/v2/sectors` list endpoint (a different, non-rate-limited path) did work and confirmed "Transportation/Logistics" as the exact registered sector tag.

Step 2 supplements: ransomlook.io's `/api/search` endpoint returned HTTP 400 Bad Request for the query attempted (likely a different expected query-parameter format not documented publicly) — treated as unavailable, skipped gracefully. ransomwhat.telemetry.ltd/posts.json redirected to ransomwatch.telemetry.ltd, which turned out to be an archived/no-longer-maintained project page with no live claim data — also skipped gracefully; noted as unavailable rather than fabricated.

All 8 example incidents were independently verified via multiple WebSearch queries and cross-referenced against named news/breach-tracking sources (Forbes, CNBC, TechTarget, SEC EDGAR filings for Expeditors, The Record, BleepingComputer, TechRadar, The Register, ClassAction.org, CNN, Maritime Executive, therecord.media) rather than relying solely on ransomware.live's short descriptions. Aggregate stats were pulled via WebSearch against Sophos, Coveware, Verizon DBIR, Comparitech, and Zscaler ThreatLabz reporting; IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025 was checked but did not surface a clean global (non-India-specific) transportation-industry cost figure in available search snippets, so it was omitted rather than approximated.

example_incidents.group: NotPetya (masqueraded as Petya ransomware; attributed to Sandworm/Russian military intelligence, not a typical criminal ransomware gang)
example_incidents.summary: The NotPetya wiper, disguised as ransomware, spread globally via a compromised Ukrainian accounting software update (M.E.Doc) and crippled Maersk's global IT infrastructure, forcing the reinstallation of roughly 4,000 servers and 45,000 PCs and halting container booking and port operations across multiple countries.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Maersk publicly estimated total costs of $200-300 million (lost revenue, IT restoration, and extraordinary operating costs), disclosed in investor communications; widely cited as one of the costliest cyber incidents in history at the time.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not applicable in the traditional sense — NotPetya had no functioning decryption mechanism; no ransom was viably payable or paid despite a nominal $300 in Bitcoin demanded on-screen.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Core systems were down for roughly 10 days; a full IT rebuild (including a 'miracle' surviving domain controller found in Ghana) took an emergency response team working around the clock roughly a week to restore booking systems, with normal port operations taking longer to stabilize.
example_incidents.data_impact: Primarily an operational/availability impact (systems wiped) rather than a data-exfiltration/breach event; no large-scale customer PII exposure was reported.

example_incidents.group: Mailto (Netwalker family) initially; Nefilim in the second, follow-on attack
example_incidents.summary: Australian freight and logistics giant Toll Group was hit by ransomware twice within three months in 2020. The first attack infected roughly 1,000 servers and forced a full network shutdown; the second (Nefilim, a double-extortion group) again took down the MyToll customer portal and stole and threatened to leak data.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as a specific dollar figure by Toll Group; operational disruption affected freight booking, invoicing, and customer service for weeks across both incidents.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed; Toll Group stated it did not pay.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: First attack: core IT systems and ~1,000 servers taken offline, with a multi-week recovery of booking/tracking portals. Second attack (three months later): MyToll portal and other systems again disrupted for an extended period while freight shipments continued via manual workarounds.
example_incidents.data_impact: Nefilim attackers stole and published approximately 220GB of data from at least one server, including current and former employee information.

example_incidents.group: Not publicly attributed to a named ransomware group in company disclosures
example_incidents.summary: Global freight forwarder Expeditors International proactively shut down most of its global operating systems after detecting a cyberattack, disrupting its ability to move shipments through ports and process customer orders for weeks, with effects disclosed as materially impacting quarterly results in SEC filings.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Per SEC 10-K/8-K filings: approximately $62 million in incremental demurrage charges (inability to timely move shipments through ports) and approximately $28 million in investigation, recovery, and remediation expenses in H1 2022 — commonly summarized in press coverage as roughly $60 million in total incident-related costs; company also disclosed lower shipment volumes and revenue impact as customers shifted to competitors during the outage.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Systems were shut down company-wide starting February 20, 2022; recovery of operating and accounting systems extended over several weeks, with the company still describing 'material adverse impact' months later in its Q1 2022 disclosures.
example_incidents.data_impact: Not detailed in public filings as a large-scale data breach; disclosures focused primarily on operational/financial impact rather than confirmed record counts of exposed data.

example_incidents.victim: Port of Nagoya (Nagoya Harbor Transportation Association / Nagoya United Terminal System)
example_incidents.group: LockBit 3.0 (claimed credit; not officially confirmed by port authorities)
example_incidents.summary: Japan's largest and busiest cargo port (handling ~10% of Japan's trade volume, including Toyota vehicle exports) suffered a ransomware attack on its Nagoya Port Unified Terminal System (NUTS), the central OT/IT system managing container terminal operations, halting all container loading/unloading operations.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly quantified in dollar terms; impact described qualitatively as significant given the port's role in ~10% of Japan's total trade volume and its handling of major automotive exports (Toyota).
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Container operations were fully suspended for roughly 2-3 days (attack detected July 4, most terminals resumed by July 6) after servers were isolated and systems restored from backup.
example_incidents.data_impact: Primarily an OT/operational-availability incident (terminal management system encrypted); no large-scale personal data exposure was publicly reported.

example_incidents.summary: Akira ransomware operators brute-forced a weak employee password (no MFA in place) to breach 158-year-old UK haulage firm KNP Logistics, encrypting critical systems and data. The already financially strained company was unable to secure emergency investment in the aftermath and entered administration roughly three months later.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not disclosed as a precise incident-remediation cost; the ultimate financial outcome was total business collapse — KNP Logistics Group entered insolvency/administration, with the ransomware attack cited by administrators as a decisive contributing factor alongside pre-existing market pressures.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Ransom demand reported at approximately GBP 5 million (some reporting cites GBP 5-6 million); not paid.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Critical operational and financial systems were encrypted and unusable; the company was unable to recover operationally and ceased trading roughly three months after the attack rather than completing a technical recovery.
example_incidents.data_impact: Financial and operational data was encrypted/compromised; approximately 730 employees lost their jobs when the company subsequently collapsed into administration.

example_incidents.summary: Major North American less-than-truckload (LTL) freight carrier Estes Express Lines was breached by the LockBit ransomware gang, which stole personal data and later published it on its leak site after Estes declined to pay. Estes disclosed the breach to regulators and affected individuals over the following months, triggering a class-action lawsuit.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as a specific dollar figure; costs would include forensic investigation, legal defense of the resulting class action, and regulatory notification expenses.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Estes publicly stated it refused to pay the ransom; specific demand amount not disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Forensic investigation concluded November 7, 2023; notification to affected individuals began December 4, 2023 — roughly ten weeks after initial network access. Operational downtime specifics were not detailed in public reporting.
example_incidents.data_impact: Breach affected 21,184 individuals per filing with the Maine Attorney General; compromised data included names and Social Security numbers of current/former employees, job applicants, and/or customers. LockBit published the stolen data on its leak site November 13, 2023.

The sector has seen some of history's costliest cyber incidents (Maersk/NotPetya, ~$300M) as well as cases where a ransomware attack directly caused a long-established company's insolvency (KNP Logistics, ~730 jobs lost). Live ransomware.live tracking shows a very high and steadily growing victim count across trucking, freight forwarding, maritime/port operators, warehousing, and fleet-technology vendors, spanning dozens of active ransomware groups and dozens of countries. Industry reporting for 2025 shows both attack frequency (+34% YoY) and average ransom demands (+685% YoY, to $2.19M) rising sharply, with third-party/supply-chain exposure (shared ELD, TMS, and port-terminal software) acting as a key amplifier — a single vendor compromise can cascade operational disruption across many otherwise-unrelated carriers simultaneously.
